archetype.name: Retooling (offense ahead of defense)
archetype.definition: A second-year Kellen Moore team whose young quarterback has lifted the offense to league average while the defense has fallen apart, leaving a below-average team in a division so weak that the record still matters.

report.headline: A real passing offense undone by giveaways and a defense that leaks deep
report.take:
The Saints are a team swapping one problem for another. Last year the offense was the anchor, 18 points a game and 28th in the league, while the defense held up (10th in EPA allowed). This year Tyler Shough has started every game, the offense is up to 23.1 points a game (15th), and the defense has slid to 23rd in EPA allowed and 27th in points allowed. Net EPA ranks 26th, and the 3-5 record is about what the play deserves: the point differential implies 3.7 wins, so there is no hard-luck story here.

The offense runs through Shough's arm and Chris Olave's 83 targets, behind a line that protects well (9th in pressure rate allowed) and rarely gets flagged. What keeps it from being good is the ball. Fifteen giveaways and a -6 turnover differential have turned productive games into losses: 410 passing yards in Detroit came with three turnovers in a one-point loss, and four giveaways sank the Raiders game. The run game is no help. 3.29 yards a carry and a 31st-ranked success rate, with backs getting 2.11 yards before contact, means the line is not opening anything and Shough has to carry almost every drive.

The defense's numbers flatter it in one spot and expose it everywhere else. Twenty-three sacks rank 10th, but the pressure rate is 31st; this unit turns very few pressures into sacks at a rate that rarely holds. Behind that weak rush the secondary is the league's worst against deep passes, 27th in explosive pass rate allowed, and opponents convert 47.2% of third downs (28th). Missed tackles (26th) extend plays that should end. If the sack conversions cool off, there is nothing underneath to hold the line.

Where it goes from here is unusually open, because the entire NFC South sits at 3-5 or 3-6. Sunday's game against Carolina is a true swing game. A brutal stretch against Chicago, Cincinnati and Green Bay follows, then a closing run of mostly division games against teams just as flawed. The Saints do not have to be good to stay in the race, just less error-prone than three other mediocre teams, and the turnovers are the thing standing in the way.

strengths.title: Clean pockets for Shough
strengths.body: The line keeps Shough upright: 9th in pressure rate allowed and 10th in QB hit rate. That is why the passing game can produce big afternoons like the 10.9 and 10.6 pass-EPA games against Baltimore and Pittsburgh. It has been stable all year, but center Erik McCoy (97% of snaps) is now hurt, and how the line holds up without him is the open question.

strengths.title: Aggressive and efficient in short yardage
strengths.body: Moore goes for it on fourth down more than anyone (1st in go rate), and the offense backs it up by converting 80% of short-yardage tries (4th). That aggressiveness adds possessions an offense this inconsistent badly needs. It is a coaching identity rather than a hot streak, so it should hold.

strengths.title: Disciplined, few free yards
strengths.body: At 6.1 penalties a game (5th fewest) and 2.5 line penalties (4th), the Saints rarely beat themselves with flags, which keeps drives on schedule for a run game that cannot dig out of long-yardage downs. Discipline like this tends to be a stable team trait.

concerns.title: Giveaways keep erasing good offense
concerns.body: Fifteen turnovers and a -6 differential (25th per game) are the clearest difference between this team and a .500 one. Several of them came in otherwise productive games, so this is a young-quarterback and ball-security problem, not an offense that can't move the ball. Turnover rates usually drift toward average, so there is some upside, but nothing in the log yet shows the problem easing.

concerns.title: No pass rush, burned deep
concerns.body: The defense ranks 31st in pressure rate and dead last in EPA allowed on deep passes, a combination that leaves corners exposed on long developing throws. The 23 sacks hide how rarely this rush actually gets home, and that conversion rate is likely to regress. Third downs (28th) and missed tackles (26th) round out a unit whose decline from last season's 10th-ranked EPA defense looks real, not like a fluke.

concerns.title: A run game that goes nowhere
concerns.body: 3.29 yards a carry (29th) and a 33.3% success rate (31st), with backs averaging 2.11 yards before contact, point at the blocking rather than the ball carriers. Losing McCoy at center and having Travis Etienne on IR and CJ Donaldson out leaves Kendre Miller and Alvin Kamara behind a weaker interior. Expect this to get worse before it gets better.

trend.note: Wins and losses have alternated with no streak longer than three, and the passing game has swung from 10.9 EPA at Baltimore to -11.9 against Minnesota to 10.6 against Pittsburgh. The most recent win over Cleveland came by one point despite two giveaways and five sacks allowed, so there's no real sign of the team settling.

nextGame.headline: Depleted Panthers secondary meets Shough in a pivotal division coin flip
nextGame.body:
Two 3-5 teams in a division with no winning record, and the Book has it close: Saints -1.5, total 47.5. Carolina throws more than almost anyone given the situation (3rd in pass rate over expected) behind a line that allows pressure constantly (30th), but the Saints' rush is 31st in pressure rate, so the matchup hinges on whether New Orleans keeps turning its rare pressures into sacks. Going the other way, Carolina has the league's weakest pass rush (32nd in sack rate and QB hit rate) and keeps the ball in front of it (2nd in explosive pass rate allowed). It also takes the ball away (13 takeaways, 5th) and folds in the red zone (29th) and on third down (31st). That plays to a Saints offense that protects well, converts short yardage and can grind out long drives if it holds onto the ball.

Availability tilts toward New Orleans in the secondary but against it up front. The Saints are likely without center Erik McCoy, listed questionable but described by Moore as out "for a little bit," and with Etienne on IR and Donaldson out, Miller and Kamara carry the backfield. Carolina is far more banged up: linebackers Bobby Okereke and Jaelan Phillips are out, corners Jaycee Horn and Mike Jackson are on IR with Will Lee III out, and guard Damien Lewis is out with Brady Christensen on IR. Xavier Legette may return from IR to give Bryce Young another target.

waysToWin.title: Pick apart a gutted, rushless secondary
waysToWin.body: With Horn, Lee and Jackson unavailable and the league's worst pass rush in front of them, Shough should have time against backup corners. Carolina's stingy numbers against opposing WR1s were built with a healthier secondary, so Olave has a real chance to break through. Clean pockets plus thin coverage is the Saints' best path.

waysToWin.title: Work the tight end and backs
waysToWin.body: Carolina has been soft against tight ends and lead backs as receivers, both 27th in PPR points over average, and it is missing Okereke and Phillips at linebacker. Juwan Johnson and Kamara as a receiver give Shough short, safe completions that also cut down the turnover risk.

waysToWin.title: Finish drives with fourth-down aggression
waysToWin.body: Carolina's defense is 31st on third down and 29th in red-zone touchdown rate, and Moore's league-leading fourth-down aggressiveness fits that weakness. Turning long drives into touchdowns rather than field goals is how the Saints win a close shootout.

waysToLose.title: Feeding Carolina's takeaway habit
waysToLose.body: Carolina's defense doesn't sack anyone, but it ranks 5th in takeaways, and the Saints have given the ball away 15 times. One or two short fields would wipe out the protection edge. This is the most likely way the Saints lose a game they should control.

waysToLose.title: Bryce Young throws over the top
waysToLose.body: A pass-heavy Carolina attack meets the defense that is last against deep throws and 27th in explosive passes allowed. Carolina's line allows pressure constantly and is missing guard Lewis, but if the Saints' weak rush can't exploit it, Young will have time to push the ball downfield.

waysToLose.title: Offense stalls without McCoy
waysToLose.body: The run game was already near the bottom of the league with McCoy playing nearly every snap. A new center and a thinned backfield could make the Saints one-dimensional and invite third-and-long, where Shough's turnover risk spikes.

nextGame.watch: Shough's ball security: Carolina can't get to him and is missing three corners, so a giveaway-free game should be enough for the Saints to win.

restOfSeason.body:
The offense should stay roughly league average, since Shough's protection and the fourth-down aggressiveness are durable traits. McCoy's absence and the run game drag on it, and the coming stretch of Chicago, Cincinnati and Green Bay, plus two games against Tampa Bay's 2nd-ranked defense, will push scoring down from 23.1 a game. The turnover count is the most likely thing to improve simply because rates this bad usually ease, and that is the Saints' main source of upside.

The defense is the bigger worry. Its sack total depends on a conversion rate that rarely holds behind a 31st-ranked pressure rate, and once that cools the deep-ball and third-down problems will show more. Still, the division is wide open and much of the closing schedule is against teams with records just like theirs. A finish in the 6-8 win range with an outside shot at the division is the honest picture.
swingFactors: Whether the sacks keep coming without pressure

confidence.note: Eight games with one starting QB, but the McCoy injury, backfield losses and a sack rate likely to regress add uncertainty.
